query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled annealing treatment that induces the in-situ formation of a finely dispersed, ductile secondary phase (e.g., a Mn- or Fe-rich intermetallic) along the grain boundaries will arrest crack propagation and enhance mechanical robustness without compromising the caloric response of the (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38, which exhibits coarse grain boundaries and brittle intergranular cracking despite high caloric performance.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled annealing treatment tailored to promote the formation of a fine, ductile secondary phase preferentially at grain boundaries.
generation.conditions: Under similar applied magnetic/pressure fields and thermal cycling around 300–400 K as used in prior caloric tests; mechanical loading conditions (cyclic compression tests) akin to those in previous studies.
generation.structural_mediator: Finely dispersed ductile intermetallic precipitates formed in situ along grain boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The precipitates serve as crack blunting and bridging agents, refining the grain structure and mitigating crack initiation and propagation. This microstructural modification succeeds in improving compressive strength and toughness without altering the intrinsic caloric phase transformation behavior.
generation.predicted_outcome: The annealed alloy is expected to exhibit a significant improvement in compressive strength (targeting values above ~150 MPa compared to the untreated sample) and enhanced ductility while retaining its large caloric response under applied fields.
generation.baseline: Untreated (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 with high caloric response but poor mechanical integrity and prone to cracking.
generation.boundary: The improvement is predicted under applied magnetic/pressure fields and thermal cycles (approximately 300–400 K) with cyclic mechanical loads, conditions under which the caloric effect is normally maintained.
generation.uncertainty: The precise quantitative improvements in strength and toughness, as well as the long-term stability of the induced microstructure under cyclic loading, remain uncertain until experimentally verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy samples: one set undergoes the controlled annealing treatment to induce ductile precipitates while the other remains in the as-cast state. Subject both sets to identical conditions involving applied magnetic/pressure fields, thermal cycling around 300–400 K, and cyclic mechanical loading.
measurements: Compressive strength and ductility via mechanical testing
Caloric response evaluation under applied fields (e.g., measurement of temperature change)
Microstructural analysis using SEM/TEM to verify formation and distribution of the secondary phase
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show statistically significant improvements in compressive strength (e.g., failing to exceed ~150 MPa beyond the untreated material) or if the caloric response is substantially degraded relative to the control, then the hypothesis is falsified.

The microstructure, mechanical, and tribological properties of the composites were investigated. Based on the test and analysis, the following conclusions can be drawn: 1. The distribution of HEA phase is relatively uniform after SPS. Under the high temperature SPS process, elemental diffusion occurs between the matrix phase and the HEA reinforcement phase. The addition of HEA will decrease the grain size of the composites and generate some Al2O3 particles at the grain boundary. 2. The density and hardness of the composites increase with the increasing of HEA content. Both the ultimate compressive strength and yield strength increase remarkably with an increasing weight fraction of the HEA. frame.system: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high‐entropy alloy in its as‐fabricated, bulk form exhibits an excellent caloric response under applied magnetic/pressure fields, but its microstructure leads to poor mechanical integrity (crack initiation and propagation).
frame.goal: To achieve robust mechanical integrity (enhanced toughness and compressive strength) without reducing the high caloric effect, while keeping the alloy formulation rare‐earth free.
frame.limitation: The material tends to crack and shows poor integrity, limiting its practical application despite its caloric performance.
root_cause_cues: gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved
constraints: The intervention must be a single-step modification
It should not sacrifice the caloric response
The alloy must remain free of rare earths
frame.regime: The alloy is intended to operate under applied-field and pressure-field conditions, experiencing cyclic thermal loads around its caloric transition temperature (likely within a moderate temperature range, e.g., 300–400 K) and mechanical loading (where prior epoxy and In composites achieved compressive strengths in the range of ~48–218 MPa)
prior_attempts: Incorporation of epoxy in Mn0.98CoGe yielding compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa
Use of low-melting In composites, achieving 48 MPa compressive strength with high thermal conductivity
frame.understanding: The hypothesis involves understanding and controlling the microstructural evolution to achieve simultaneous improvement in mechanical toughness and retention of caloric performance.
frame.hypothesis: A single intervention that could overcome the limitation is to implement a controlled annealing treatment to induce in-situ formation of a finely dispersed, ductile secondary phase (e.g., a Mn- or Fe-rich intermetallic) along grain boundaries. This intervention is expected to refine the grain structure and create ductile interfacial phases that arrest crack propagation. Mechanistically, the secondary phase acts as a crack-bridging or blunting agent, which enhances toughness and compressive strength (targeting improvements relative to the brittle, unmodified alloy, for example, reaching compressive strengths on the order of 150 MPa or higher) without interfering with the intrinsic caloric phase transformation. The boundary conditions include operation under the same applied-field, pressure-field, thermal cycles (around 300–400 K), and mechanical loading conditions as the original alloy, ensuring that the caloric response remains robust. Supporting prior evidence comes from related MM′X materials where microstructural engineering such as second-phase toughening has improved mechanical properties. A decisive controlled experiment could involve processing two sets of the alloy – one with the controlled annealing treatment to induce the ductile phase and one without – and then subjecting both to identical caloric, mechanical (compressive stress tests), thermal cycling, and field application conditions. If the annealed sample fails to show statistically significant improvements in compressive strength (e.g., below the target improvement over the unchanged alloy) or if its caloric response deteriorates notably compared to the control, the hypothesis would be falsified.
